declared_non_coverage: R12-1a (declared, not fixed): dependency-cruiser 16.10.4 builds its set of followable extensions once per run from the first successful resolution (src/extract/resolve/module-classifiers.mjs), and retries a '.js' specifier that resolves to nothing against '.ts', '.tsx' and '.d.ts' only. When the first resolution is the NodeNext pattern (an './x.js' import of x.ts), '.js', '.mjs' and '.cjs' stop being followable for the whole run, so a '.mjs' bridge OUTSIDE the four source roots becomes a leaf and its edges are not judged by rules 1 and 6. The trigger is the first ordinary app file under apps/. The reviewer read the cause from the source and observed the effect; neither was reproduced here. The plants added by this change sit inside services/api/src, so they do not cover it.

R12-1b (declared, not fixed): a bridge file in a folder outside the four source roots (a lib/ folder, or a file at the repository root) is followed but judged only by rules that key on a source-root path, so a transit through it escapes rules 2, 4, 5 and 7.

R12-1c (declared, not fixed): pnpm 11 installs a 'file:' dependency on a test package as a copy under the root node_modules, so an import of that package from a service resolves to a path no rule judges and rule 6 never sees it. A 'link:' dependency resolves into tests/ and is judged. check:modules does not refuse a 'file:' specifier or dependenciesMeta.injected.

R12-1, why it matters and why it is left: production-options.test.mjs copies only the four source roots, so every import out of them resolves to nothing there, and the 'no unplanted violation' assertion trips on any legitimate npm import from a source root; the first runtime dependency forces that copy or assertion to change, and until (a) to (c) are closed (a) to (c) are silent bypasses in CI's real-tree check. This change does not alter that.

R12-3 (declared, not fixed): a computed dynamic import() (for example import() of a path joined at run time), or createRequire bound to any name other than 'require', reaches internals at runtime and is invisible to every rule; the backstop reports a createRequire call only when it is bound to the name require. This is the inherent limit of static analysis. A lint rule that refuses a non-literal import() or createRequire in first-party source, or dependency-cruiser's exoticRequireStrings, would close part of it; both are a new rule and not an agent's decision, and exoticRequireStrings would add an option key the pin now refuses until the test is changed.

A doNotFollow or exclude loosening for one root AND one form (for example '^apps/.*[.]cjs$') is caught by the pin, not by a plant.
